chapters.name: Chapter 1: How solar works and how to stay safe

lessons.title: Lesson 1: The parts of a home solar system
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Name the main parts of a grid-tied solar system and say what each one does.
This lesson builds toward: Given a drawing or list of the parts of a grid-tied home solar system, you will name each main part and say what it does, getting at least 5 of 6 parts right.
Solar panels, also called modules, turn sunlight into electricity. The kind of electricity they make is direct current (DC). Homes use alternating current (AC), so an inverter changes DC into AC.
The panels sit on racking, a metal frame bolted to the roof or set on the ground. Wires run from the panels to the inverter, then to the home's main electrical panel. Disconnect switches let workers shut parts of the system off. A meter counts the electricity the home uses and sends to the grid.
Most home systems are grid-tied: they stay connected to the power company's lines, called the grid. Extra power can flow to the grid, and the home uses grid power at night. Some homes also add a battery to store power for later or for outages.
Words to know:
- Solar panel (module): a flat panel that turns sunlight into electricity.
- PV (photovoltaic): the technology that makes electricity from light; solar panels are PV panels.
- DC (direct current): electricity that flows one way, like from a battery or a solar panel.
- AC (alternating current): electricity that changes direction many times a second; homes use AC.
- Inverter: the box that changes DC from the panels into AC for the home.
- Racking: the metal frame that holds the panels.
- Grid-tied: connected to the power company's lines.
- Disconnect: a switch that cuts power to part of a system.
Official sources:
- U.S. Department of Energy: Homeowner's Guide to Going Solar
Try it now: On paper, draw a simple house with panels on the roof. Draw and label six boxes in order: panels, racking, inverter, disconnect, main electrical panel, meter. Next to each one, write one short line about what it does. Then cover your labels and say each part out loud.
You can now name the main parts of a grid-tied solar system and say what each one does.

check.q: Which part changes DC from the panels into AC for the home?
check.why: The inverter changes the panels' DC into the AC that homes use.

options: The system is connected to the power company's lines
The panels are tied down with rope
The system only works at night
check.why: A grid-tied system stays connected to the utility grid, so extra power can flow out and grid power can flow in.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Staying safe on a solar job site
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: List the main hazards on a solar job and the safety step for each one.
This lesson builds toward: Given a practice solar job scenario, you will list the hazards and the safety step for each one, naming falls, electric shock, heat and lifting, with a correct safety step for each.
Falls are the biggest danger in solar work. In construction, OSHA requires fall protection when you work 6 feet or more above a lower level. On a roof that usually means a personal fall arrest system: a full-body harness, a lanyard and a roof anchor, set up by a trained person. Inspect your harness before every use.
Electric shock is the second big danger. Solar panels make electricity whenever light hits them, and you cannot switch the sun off. Wires from the panels can be live in daylight even when a switch is off. As a new helper you do not connect or touch wiring: only qualified, trained workers do electrical work, following lockout and tagout steps.
Ladders: set them on firm, level ground, have the side rails reach at least 3 feet above the roof edge, and keep three points of contact. Heat: drink water often, rest in the shade, and tell your lead if you feel dizzy or sick. Lifting: panels are big and catch the wind, so carry them with two people and lift with your legs.
Wear your protective gear (PPE): hard hat, safety glasses, work gloves and boots with good grip. Stop work and tell your lead whenever something feels unsafe.
Step by step:
- Before you climb: check the ladder, the weather and your harness.
- On the roof: stay tied off to an anchor whenever you are 6 feet or more up.
- Treat every panel and wire as live; do not touch connections unless you are qualified.
- Drink water, take shade breaks and lift panels with a partner.
- Stop and tell your lead about any hazard.
Words to know:
- OSHA: the U.S. Occupational Safety and Health Administration, the federal agency for workplace safety.
- Fall protection: gear and setups that stop you from falling or stop a fall safely.
- Personal fall arrest system: a full-body harness, a lanyard and an anchor that catch you if you fall.
- PPE: personal protective equipment: safety gear you wear, like a hard hat and gloves.
- Lockout/tagout: steps that shut off and lock power so no one can turn it back on while work is done.
- Live: carrying electricity.
Official sources:
- OSHA: Fall protection
- OSHA: 29 CFR 1926.501, duty to have fall protection (construction)
- OSHA: 29 CFR 1926.1053, ladders
- OSHA: Heat
- U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics: Solar photovoltaic installers
Try it now: Practice scenario: it is a hot July morning. Your crew is putting 18 panels on a two-story roof. The ladder is on soft grass, one coworker has no harness, and a panel's wires are hanging loose. On paper, make a two-column checklist: Hazard and Safety step. Write at least four rows (falls, shock, heat, lifting, and the ladder).
You can now spot the main hazards on a solar job and name the safety step for each one.

check.q: In construction, at what height does OSHA require fall protection?
options: Only on the top of the roof
check.why: OSHA's construction rule calls for fall protection at 6 feet or more above a lower level.

check.q: It is sunny and the disconnect switch is off. Are the panel wires safe to touch?
options: Yes, the switch makes everything safe
No, panels make power whenever light hits them, so treat wires as live
Yes, if you wear work gloves
Only if the inverter is quiet
check.why: Panels keep making electricity in light, so wires from them can still be live.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Basic solar math (practice only)
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Calculate watts, system size and string voltage from practice numbers.
This lesson builds toward: Given practice numbers for panels, volts and amps, you will calculate watts, system size and string voltage, with no math errors, showing your work.
Crews use a few simple formulas every day. All the numbers in this lesson are made up for practice only. Real designs use the panel's label, the manufacturer's data sheet and the electrical code, and are checked by a qualified designer.
Power: watts = volts x amps. A practice panel making 40 volts at 10 amps makes 40 x 10 = 400 watts. 1,000 watts is 1 kilowatt (kW).
System size: number of panels x watts per panel. 20 practice panels at 400 watts each = 8,000 watts, which is 8 kW.
Strings: panels wired in series form a string. In series, the voltages add and the amps stay the same. Three practice panels at 40 volts each in series = 120 volts. In parallel, the amps add and the voltage stays the same.
Step by step:
- Write the formula first.
- Put in the numbers with their units (V, A, W).
- Do the math on a calculator.
- Change watts to kilowatts by dividing by 1,000.
- Check: does the answer make sense?
Words to know:
- Volt (V): a measure of electrical push or pressure.
- Amp (A): a measure of how much electricity is flowing.
- Watt (W): a measure of power: volts times amps.
- Kilowatt (kW): 1,000 watts.
- Series: wired end to end in one line; voltages add.
- Parallel: wired side by side; amps add.
- String: a group of panels wired in series.
Try it now: Practice only. Solve on paper and show your work: (a) A panel makes 36 volts at 11 amps. How many watts? (b) A home has 24 panels of 350 watts. What is the system size in kW? (c) Five panels at 40 volts each are wired in series. What is the string voltage? Answers to check yourself: (a) 396 W, (b) 8,400 W = 8.4 kW, (c) 200 V.
You can now calculate watts, system size and string voltage from practice numbers and show your work.

check.q: Practice only: 15 panels at 400 watts each. What is the system size?
Practice only: four panels at 40 volts each are wired in series. What is the string voltage?
check.why: In series the voltages add: 4 x 40 V = 160 V.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: From the roof to your first job

lessons.title: Lesson 4: The steps of a rooftop install
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Put the steps of a rooftop solar install in order and say who does each one.
This lesson builds toward: Given the steps of a rooftop solar install in mixed order, you will put the steps in the right order and say who does each one, with no more than one step out of place.
Every install follows a path. First, a site assessment: someone checks the roof's age and condition, which way it faces, shade from trees, and the home's electrical panel. Then a designer lays out the panels and the wiring.
Next comes the permit. The city or county building department reviews the plans before work starts. On install day, the crew sets up safety gear, marks the roof, and fastens roof attachments into the rafters. Each attachment is flashed and sealed so the roof does not leak. Then the crew bolts on the racking and mounts the panels.
A qualified electrician or licensed worker makes the electrical connections, following the National Electrical Code (NEC) and the local rules. Then the system is inspected by the local building official. Finally, the utility (power company) approves the system to connect to the grid, often called permission to operate. Only then is the system turned on.
Helpers mostly carry and stage materials, help set racking and panels, keep the site clean, and follow the lead's instructions.
Step by step:
- Site assessment: roof, direction, shade, electrical panel.
- Design: panel layout and wiring plan.
- Permit from the city or county.
- Safety setup, then roof attachments, flashed and sealed.
- Racking, then panels mounted.
- Electrical connections by qualified workers.
- Inspection by the local official.
- Utility approval (permission to operate), then turn on.
Words to know:
- Site assessment: a visit to check whether a roof or yard is right for solar.
- Permit: official permission from the city or county to do the work.
- Flashing: metal or other material that keeps water out where something goes through the roof.
- Rafter: one of the wood beams that hold up a roof.
- NEC: the National Electrical Code (NFPA 70), the rules for safe electrical work that states and cities adopt.
- Inspection: a check by an official that the work meets the code.
- Permission to operate: the power company's OK to turn on a grid-tied system.
Official sources:
- U.S. Department of Energy: Homeowner's Guide to Going Solar
- NFPA 70: National Electrical Code (check which edition your state uses)
Try it now: Write each of the 8 install steps on its own small piece of paper. Mix them up, then put them back in order without looking at the lesson. Next to each one, write who does it: designer, city or county, crew, qualified electrician, inspector or utility. Check your order against the lesson.
You can now list the steps of a rooftop solar install in order and say who does each one.

check.q: What usually comes right before install day?
check.why: The city or county permit comes before work starts on the roof.

check.q: Why are roof attachments flashed and sealed?
options: So the roof does not leak
To make the panels produce more power
check.why: Flashing and sealing keep water out where bolts go through the roof.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Credentials, licenses and training
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: List the credentials and licenses for entry-level solar work where you live, with the official source for each.
This lesson builds toward: Using the official NABCEP and state websites, you will list the credentials and licenses for entry-level solar work where you live, naming the source page for each one.
Many installers start as helpers and learn on the job, often for one month to a year. Some take a short course at a community college, technical school or apprenticeship program first. Electricians, roofers and construction workers can often move into solar faster.
NABCEP (the North American Board of Certified Energy Practitioners) offers well-known solar credentials. The entry-level one is the NABCEP PV Associate. You can qualify by finishing a course with a NABCEP Associate Registered Training Provider, or by showing at least six months of full-time solar work, and then passing the exam. Later, experienced installers can aim for NABCEP Board Certification, such as PV Installation Professional.
Licenses are set by states, and some cities. Some states require a solar or electrical license for certain work; others do not. Fees, exam rules and requirements change, so check the official NABCEP page and your state licensing board yourself before you pay for anything.
This course prepares you to start. It does not give you a credential or a license.
Step by step:
- Read the NABCEP Associate program page.
- Find a registered training provider or count your solar work months.
- Search your state's contractor or electrical licensing board for solar rules.
- Write down each requirement and the page where you found it.
- Ask local solar employers which credentials they want.
Words to know:
- NABCEP: the North American Board of Certified Energy Practitioners, which offers solar credentials.
- Credential: proof that you passed a test or met a standard.
- License: permission from a state or city to do certain work.
- Apprenticeship: a paid job with training, where you learn from skilled workers.
- Registered training provider: a school NABCEP lists as approved to prepare you for its associate exam.
Official sources:
- NABCEP: Associate program (PV Associate)
- NABCEP: Certifications
- U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics: How to become a solar photovoltaic installer
- CareerOneStop: License Finder
Try it now: Open the NABCEP Associate program page and write down the ways to qualify for the PV Associate. Then search your state name plus "solar contractor license" and find your state's official licensing board page (it often ends in .gov). Write one line on what it says, and the web address.
You can now name the entry-level NABCEP credential, say how to qualify for it, and find your state's licensing rules on the official page.

check.q: Which is NABCEP's entry-level solar PV credential?
check.why: The NABCEP PV Associate is the entry-level solar PV credential.

check.q: Where do you check whether your state requires a license for solar work?
options: An ad for a fast online course
Your state's official licensing board page
check.why: Licenses are set by each state, so the state's official board page is the source to trust.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Your Solar Start Plan
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Write a Solar Start Plan with dates and a résumé skills section.
This lesson builds toward: Using your notes from this course, you will write a Solar Start Plan with dates and a résumé skills section, meeting every row of the rubric.
Now put it all together into one page you can take to a training program or an interview. A plan with real dates shows an employer you are serious.
Your plan has six parts: how solar works in your own words; a safety checklist; two practice math problems with your work shown; the install steps in order; your credential path with dates and sources; and a "Solar skills" résumé section.
For the résumé section, write true things you can do now, in short bullets that start with an action word. For example: "Know the parts of a grid-tied PV system and how DC becomes AC." "Trained in solar job site hazards: fall protection, shock, heat and safe lifting." "Can calculate system size and string voltage." Add past work that helps: construction, roofing, military, warehouse or any job with tools, heights or teamwork.
Veterans and people with a record: many solar employers hire from these groups. Be honest on applications, and ask a local workforce center or reentry program about training help.
Step by step:
- Write your 3 to 4 sentence explanation of a grid-tied system.
- Copy your safety checklist from Lesson 2 and finish it.
- Add two practice math problems with your work.
- List the 8 install steps in order.
- Write your credential path with target dates and source pages.
- Write 3 résumé bullets that start with an action word.
Words to know:
- Résumé: a short document that lists your skills, work and training for employers.
- Target date: the day you plan to finish a step.
- Workforce center: a free public office that helps people find jobs and training; many are called American Job Centers.
Official sources:
- CareerOneStop: Find an American Job Center
Try it now: Final task: make your one-page Solar Start Plan with all six parts. Put a real date next to every credential and job step, and the web address for each requirement you checked. Read your résumé bullets out loud as if you were in an interview.
You can now show an employer or training program a written plan for starting solar work, with dates, sources and a résumé skills section.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds How solar works The explanation misses the inverter or mixes up AC and DC. Names panels, racking, inverter, disconnect, meter and the grid, and says what each does. Also explains, in their own words, why the disconnect matters for safety during service and why panels are live whenever there is daylight. Safety checklist Misses falls or electric shock, or gives no safety step. Lists falls, shock, heat and lifting, each with a correct safety step (including fall protection at 6 feet). Adds ladder setup and a stop-work rule, and says who to tell. Practice math A math error, or no work shown. Both problems are right, with the formula and units shown. Also checks that each answer makes sense and changes watts to kW correctly. Install steps Two or more steps out of order, or the permit or inspection is missing. All 8 steps in order, with at most one out of place, and who does each. Explains why flashing and the utility's approval matter. Credential path No dates, or requirements with no source. Names the NABCEP PV Associate and a way to qualify, plus the state licensing check, each with a target date and web address. Names a specific registered training provider or local employer and a backup plan. Résumé section Bullets are vague or claim a license or credential the learner does not have. Three true bullets that start with an action word and match solar work. Connects past work (construction, military, warehouse) to solar tasks. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Which is the best résumé bullet for a solar helper job?
options: "Trained in solar job site hazards: fall protection, shock, heat and safe lifting."
check.why: It is true, specific and starts with an action word; never claim a license you do not have.

check.q: What makes a Solar Start Plan stronger?
options: Real target dates and the source page for each requirement
No dates, so you stay flexible
check.why: Dates and official sources turn a wish into a plan an employer can trust.
